body.p: Hannah Yarnall Journal of a Visit to Canada 1803

div.p: Set out upon a journey to visit Friends in Canada, at Black Creek Pelham and Young street. And took leave of my family about 9 o’clock, excepting my son James who accompanied me all the way to Pelham and several of my Friends as far as Frankford, where dear Mary Witchel joined. Although the parting with our friends was solemn, yet as kind providence favored me with a quiet serene mind, it very much alleviated the trial. Proceeded to Jacob Paul’s to dine, where we joined in company with John Shoemaker and Samuel Johnson, and arrived at Roberts Harper’s Providence to lodge, 39 miles from my home. Very weary in body and mind, let down so that I could not enjoy company, together with some indisposition.

Morning, large white frost a little. Recruited Nathan Harper who accompanied us thus far on his way to the Ohio, parted with us, and John Shoemaker who lodged last night at one Cox’s in this neighborhood, with in company with Thomas Stewardson and George Nauks.
Samuel Johnson’s son James, Mary, and myself expects to fall in company with them again upon a few miles ride. 15 miles to Pots Grove where we dined. I had a hard struggle to keep my head up above the billows, but through favor I did not quite sink or loose anchor. Therefore my poor vessel was not decked. The two Johns & George propose going round by leading we over the Oly hills & to meet at Thomas Lightfoot’s at Maiden Creek. By missing our road, lodged at Mordecai Lee’s near Exeter Meetinghouse. Although very weary, my mind a little recruited.

Another smart frost so as to hurt Indian corn and Buckwheat in many places. Previous to our setting out, had a solid sitting with the family, which had a tendency to add a little to our small stack. And in riding about 15 miles meet with those three Friends we parted with yesterday. all Dined together at our valued Friend Thomas Lightfoot’s. Its proposed for us all to proceed on 12 miles to Mosers Tavern to lodge, as we cannot travel so fast in a carriage as on horseback, and leave James Wilson, Issac Coats, & Issac Bonsel to follow on tomorrow, who we expect will arrive here this evening accordingly.
It being agreed upon, we proceeded and arrived at the said place about an hour after dark a very dark and gloomy ride, especially for those in the carriage over and on the side of the blue mountain and dangerous precipices. My poor tabernacle very weary, so much so that I could not stand alone for some time after alighting from the horse. But my mind preserved quiet, and enabled to eat a hearty supper, but with not without some difficulty to set up to partake it. Sleep pretty well.

Mounted our horses about 5 o’clock this morning. Rode 12 miles to one Henry Miller’s to breakfast, over a very rough road part of the way. Had an excellent appetite. The rituals relished well, and being favored with good company has a tendency to cheer my and revive my spirits. Rode 8 miles to Hibler’s over the blue Mckay mountain and 10 miles to the next, by name Traxlers, where we got a good relish of pigeons and chickens with our chocolate. About sunset to our lodging.

Morning. James Wilson, Issac Coats, Issac Bonsal, came up and passed on to Cattawisa meeting. We stopped at Roling
Roling Creek Meeting. I was pleased with the appearance of some of the young people there, but felt pretty quiet to pass from them in silence as to myself. Mary had considerable service. After dining at Nathan Lee’s, rode 6 miles to Cattawissa, where we overtook and meet with our above said Friends. Lodged at John Loyd’s.

Morning. All set out in company. Rode 12 miles to Jersey town, and fed, and in 14 more arrived at William Ellis’s at Muncy, about 4 o’clock. Next day being rainy, we rested quiet until after dining when the rain abated. The Indian Committee set forward on their journey. We of our company feeling most easy to stop by their Preparative meeting of Muncy, which came on the next day, therefore took leave of each other with a prospect of meeting again in Canada at their Monthly Meeting.

Morning. We accordingly to prospect attended the meeting, and as I thought, Master evinced himself to be near us which for which renewed favor. I thanked him, and took fresh courage to press forward. Dined at Joseph Carpenter’s near Meetinghouse. Solid friends so posed on our way over a stream of water called Loyalsock. Also a town called Williamsport, another Newberry, and 17 miles ride. Arrived at Thomas Brown’s, whose wife was Joseph Knight’s daughter
of Burks county. After a comfortable sitting with them, we took leave and parted under the canopy of a serene quiet, which was a preparative for what followed that day. Viz.

Riding over Allegheny and Chesnut Ridge in a smart rain. 22 miles before we stopped to bathe, which was at a very little hut covered with bark. Only one room, two beds, a sick man, and no sort of a cover for our horses. Some of us very wet through our clothes. Was favored from our spirits sinking after partaking of some of our own provisions. Proceed on through the wilderness 12 miles to John Norris’s. Norris’s to very good accommodations, so much so as we could desire. They are English people. He had been educated for a teacher of their church, but I don’t know that he had officiated at anytime. they were truly kind to us, and thereby my very weary body was comforted after riding near all day in rain, and this afternoon very high mountains, each ride of us. And trees supposed to be quite 200 feet high and very thick, and in riding about 3 miles crossed a branch of Pine Creek, supposed more than 20 times.

Fine clear morning. Took our leave and proceeded on, over and by very high mountains again. In about 11 miles arrived at Moses Wilson’s, who are kind friends, much pleased to see us. Being 35 miles from meeting and 50 from Monthly meeting stayed some hours and dined on green peas & many other good things, very agreeable. Also partook of some mush mellon. They had no neighbor within 9 miles of them, in a tried situation. After leaving them, rode 9 miles to Bedford. Georges appeared poor. Haught, well meaning people. Stopped one hour
with them, then rode 2 miles to one Josiah White’s to lodge, who professed to have some claim to our society but had lost the appearance of it. They used us as well as they could I believe. and They had an elk’s horn that was between three and four feet in length.

In the morning, favored with a good degree of health, after proceeding on our way about one mile, Mary Engle felt enough easy to part from us and steer her course to the old road that she usually had traveled. But I may acknowledge it felt heavy to me looking at her lonely situation. We proceeded on the new one through the butter weeds, so high that one could not sometimes see all the company. To Buckleys 14 miles. Strawbridge new settlement. New Englanders, civil people. And there finding the receiving information that the road we were in was not opened through, was directed about 2 miles round and as is said 26 nearer than the old one would have been that Mary had turned to. We then took a mill road 14 miles through a very desolate wilderness to Tuscaroah a little new settled village. Poor enough, but made out to stay until morning, it being first day morning.

We were thoughtful about meeting, but finding the Methodists was to have one there in the fore part of the day, we thought best to proceed on our journey. Much thoughtful I felt about spending first day in traveling, and after riding some miles came to the poorest family as we thought we ever had beheld with our eyes. Some of the children naked, and one
of them had nothing but some sort of a skin on his body, and as dirty as pigs, wallowing in the road. We felt much for the poor woman who shed many tears, and appeared very thankful for our visit. Her husband was not at home. We afterwards understood that he was a very poor provider for his family, that the poor woman we supposed must suffer much at times, had moved from Jersey some years past. The next stage, after riding through as dark or the darkest part as I thought I ever was in, that was peopled to the depression of my spirits, called the old Cannaster settlement. I thought I had much rather seen neither houses nor people, excepting I could have believed they did in some degree fear their maker. Which I feared was not the case but on arriving at one Stephen’s Inn, apiece in the afternoon meet with better accommodations. And more over an old woman, their mother, which was mutually comforting she appearing rejoiced to see is said it did her good, to see us believing we were on first sight, Christian people. I had much satisfaction in conversing with her she cheered my spirits after being very near low water mark. We did not leave her children, the keepers of the inn, without reproof for suffering such a company to collect these, especially on first day like a vendue, which they appeared to be ashamed of. The poor, innocent old woman, seeing us ride up at her house, hopped over on her cane to see us, and inquire respecting our business and gave us her blessing. And I believe through her kind information we got to a very
good inn to lodge, the country considered by name Hurl. But after riding 20 miles this day (yesterday entered into York state), friendly, well-minded people, they by our permission invited several of their neighbors in after supper. And we thought had a good meeting wherein our ancient friend James was highly favored in supplication.

After a comfortable nights rest, all through favor are brave in health, and also in addition as good a breakfast as we need to have or could in reason ask for. I may acknowledge the kindness of both parents and children was such who appeared to be seeking ones, that I parted from them with reluctance. Their aged mother, who lived a piece on the road, who we stopped & took by the hand, gave us her blessing on our journey & took leave with tears on her cheeks. We have much cause to be humbly thankful under the present feeling of the supporting hand, whose promised to go before his and paint out the way. And may it not be said that here, one of the children that may be termed desolate ones, but he is omnipotent. Everywhere present, and can succor his depending ones, may it be the experience of some who we have lately parted with is the breathing of my spirit. After riding through a barren, got to Danvil about 11 o’clock. Dined on venison steaks. So on to big tree, through Janesce, where there was great preparations for training next day that we could not think of tarrying overnight as was intended. From the appearances of things we expected there was a
very disturbed house. That night we mounted our horses rode to the next stage, 40 miles, which took us an hour. In the night, very dark, got to the widow Berry’s at the ferry that crosses over the Genesee river. Good stage, and for my part I thought I had as much as nature could well bare.

In the morning, considerably rested, the waters being low, we forded the river. Soon passed through a small Indian town over a plains also by a spring that spread over some areas of ground. Fine, level road for several miles. In 22 arrived at Betavo. After putting our horses to a tavern, was kindly entertained at Jospeh Elicot’s, whose agent for the Holland Company, and his brother is judge, or was. Just as rain came on, appears to be a thriving place as to a town. But about two years since the first house was built, now a spacious courthouse & mill, with a considerable number of other buildings is erected.

Morning. Proceed through a very trying, uneven, swampy, rooty place, timber so thick and high that the sun could not shine on the road, & in 18 miles got to Vandeventer’s. A good stage, well minded people. Here we saw for the first, an Indian man. aftering Bateing, rode 12 miles to where we stayed all night. Had a pretty good ride over the plains. Here we met with many people, which appeared to be trying. All behaved civil.

In the morning, mounted our horses about sun rise. In riding 11 miles, arrived at Buffalo, where we met with a decent tavern that we
we breakfasted on beef steak, fish, and chocolate with a very good relish. Here we saw two missionaries who from New York with the Buffalo Indians, of which we saw a large number. As we rode from the town of Buffalo to the ferry along the shore of Lake Erie, it being a very fine sunshine day, many of them was fishing, some laying suning themselves, many of whom them had much silver about them in their ears noses on their breasts. And laying on their hair on their heads, some of them looked pleasant to see us, others to the reverse. In about 3 1/2 miles got to Black Rock, where the ferry is kept. Over Niagara River, which is a little below the lakes or outlet of it, is said to be 1 3/4 mile over. About 2, o’clock got into the boat, and in about 20 minutes mounted our horses on the Canada shores. Some clever settlements in view in riding a mile or two, passed by the fort where the redcoats came out to take a view of us. It seems a little trying to reflect upon being in King Georges dominions, on account in part of being so far from my acquaintances. Rode about 7 miles up the shore of the lake, and about 11 miles off from it we arrived at Daniel Pound’s of our society considerably fatigued, at Black Creek about 5 o’clock. And soon after entering under the roof I felt a degree of that comfortable quiet revive on my mind, similar to that when I lift my own habilitation, for which favor I ought to be deeply thankful for.
Seeing we cannot command such seasons, after Friends appeared rejoiced to see us. After taking a little refreshment, moved on to Asa Schoolly’s to lodge.

Feeling a freedom to see each of them in their families, Asa and wife encouraged us. He concluded to pilot us, accordingly in the morning he set out with us, excepting James Thornton, who we left at a Friend’s house, through our visit fell in with him occasionally first to Obediah Dennis’s. His mother, a tender spirited woman, second to Anna Morris’s widow, with several children and two young married women, who had not got to house-keeping, their husbands being out some distance from the house, the widow’s brothers, by name Abraham & Issac Lane. Third, to see Esther Webster, young woman. At John Moore’s, fourth. In evening, Daniel Pound’s lodged.

Morning. The above said young married men came over to see us, who appear very hopeful, and a comfortable prospect that they may be useful there. Proceeded to the fifth place, Nathan Haven’s, whose wife is Joseph Hill’s daughter sixth to Joseph Haven’s, himself disowned and very much embittered against friends. Seventh to Adam Burrel’s, his wife a very tender, spirited woman, whom we felt much near sympathy. They also have a hopeful son by name Malon, who inclines to be useful in school-keeping seventh Eighth to Joseph Marsh’s, has a lively spirited wife. things Appeared
to have things convenient in good measure so indoors & out. Marks of industry and forecast. Ninth to John Cutter’s. 10 then to Asa Schoolly’s to lodge. With them young people who have got to keeping house, makes 11 different families in this settlement of Black Creek and 62 individual members.

This morning feel I trust, at least an apprehension, I am not out of my place, which reconciles my far absence from my native land and friends desiring I may be preserved in my allotment from dishonoring the blessed truth, which I at times feel desirous above all other things to espouse. They have a meetinghouse weatherboarded but not fit to collect in. Therefore about 11 o’clock the people gathered, more than could get into the house of Asa Schoolly’s, and we believed it to be a solid profitable time. Many of the people appeared to leave us with reluctance. After dining, Asa & wife piloted us to their married son and son-in-laws, not yet members which was to our satisfaction. In the night hard rain.

About 8 o’clock in morning clouds broke, we quietly left the neighborhood in order for Belham, having Asa Schooly for our pilot. Upon riding about 20 miles down the river Niagara to the mouth of a Narrow River called Chipway, near there is several spacious buildings, two Taverns kept here. We fed after riding 2 more miles and passing by the rapids.
We came to the falls, of a very awful sight indeed. We after on our return lodged in a house two miles off it, where we felt the windows part by the great force of the fall of such a large body of water. In the evening, after riding about 40 miles, arrived at Jesse Wilson in the neighborhood of Pelham, son to Gabriel who lives in the upper parts of Jersey. His wife daughter to William Shatwell. Hopeful young couple, they have a small house but meet with comfortable entertainment which was truly acceptable, being very much fatigued notwithstanding.

We had a pretty level road in the morning. After having a religious opportunity in the family, Asa returned home. Jesse piloted us through the day second to Joshua Gillams. Third setting at Daniel Wilsons. Fourth at Thomas Rice’s. Fifth at John Taylor’s, where we lodged. Feel a renewed belief that we are in the line of the divine appointment. Nevertheless, sometimes suffer my mind to look back to my Friends & connections whom I have left. With this reflection mind the present day that will make way for the future.

Fourth day attended their Preparative meeting, under much exercise of mind way opened for some service without much relief. Afterwards, on our way to Jeremiah Moore’s, the wasps stung our horses. Mary & myself made our escape by jumping off without much hurt. After dining, walked over to their son Jacob’s, sixth. In the evening, another at Jeremiah’s, seventh. Body and spirits were down.

Morning. A little recruited had the eighth sitting at the Widow Bradshaw’s, who
who has several children, she only a member. Ninth at James Craffords near the meeting house so on to Samuel Becket’s. Before evening took a walk over to see a poor family whose wife was subject to fits, by name Thomas Gilham. Poor man was much tendered, not members among us we were led to sympathize with them. Tenth sitting at Samuel’s in evening.

Sixth day, fine clear morning. Samuel Becket accompanied us to some of the outskirts. Eleventh at John Derlin’s, his wife only a member. Twelfth at John Hill’s, whose two sisters only members, very kind. So on to Jesse Thomas’s, large family and considerable of this worlds possessions, 14 at their sons. Returned to lodge at Samuel Becket’s.

In the morning ourselves and our horses appear brave, fresh cause for thankfulness. May we be quickened under it to a watchful attention unto the painting of truth, as we have hitherto been helped to our mutual comfort so that our feelings as well as services upon comparing notes appear generally to be a link of one chain, which occasions us to feel nearly united. Returned to John Taylor’s to dine, put our horses out to rest. Afternoon visited their son John, and Samuel’s family, which makes 16. Lodged again at J. Taylor’s.

Fine weather. Attended their meeting. There was a mixed company. Trying time, no way opened for me to obtain relief to a much depressed exercised mind. But dear Mary particularly headed stood forth with some very close but pertinent remarks well fitted to the occasion as we afterwards was convinced of. Dined near meeting at James
Craffords. Rode to see a woman who had requested to join our society, which had no tendency to lessen my burden. On our return found a freedom to stop and set with a friendly family not in membership, the head of which is brother to our Friend Joycee Brekman of Burke County. And on our return to J Taylor’s, found a considerable collection of Friends. And after a time found our minds drawn into retirement, in which opportunity I experienced considerable relief to my mind. After, a comfortable night's rest.

In morning walked over to Amos Chapman’s, whose sister is a member. 17 dined at Daniel Wilson’s. Afterward rode several miles to visit Benjamin Hill 18–and Joel Bradshaws, lodged at J. Taylor’s. Philip Dennis and wife, another family makes up 19–which we missed with reluctance 3rd day

Passed this day dear Mary and myself in repairing our clothes. Towards evening the Indian Committee came, in which was truly reviving to my spirits viz. John Shoemaker, Isaac Bonsal, Issac Coats, and a young man with them from the city–George Nauks, he and I, Shoemaker tarried overnight. The two Issacs, in company with J. Wilson, went to Jeremiah Moses’s to lodge, and returned in the morning to us.

All went to monthly meeting together held at Pelham. Dear Mary opened the service in solemn supplication which was followed as I thought seasonally by J. Bonsal, in a short lively testimony, and I thought the meeting of worship closed I believed under a canopy of favor as it opened. But the meeting of discipline was a time of much close exercise,
something had through unwatchfulness got in amongst them, comparable to a tangled skein of thread, which as some of them informed us they thought if some help had not come in from some further quarter they should have been likely to have suffered much loss. We were in hopes on the whole a profitable time season. There appears a lack of study skillful workmen amongst them, although there be a few who appear well minded, and in some others much weakness was evident. Issac Bonsal dined with us at Samuel Beckett’s by candle light. 2 miles on our way towards Young Street, the rest of the Indian Committee came to us.

In the morning son James’s horse lame at Black Creek, conclude for him to return to him and endeavor to meet us here at Pelham on our return after break footing the Indian Committee. Separated not without having on our part the tender feelings touched. They set their faces forward, and with our pilot we for Young Street, but master favoring with a renewed seal of his sanction on passing on our way greatly alleviated the fresh trial. After riding 22 miles dined at one Walverton’s comfortable accommodations, kindly people. 12 miles to government houses. About 1 mile before we arrived we came to Lake Ontario. A short space from the shore there was a beautiful green bank shaded with trees which we rode under when I thought of which brought into view green bank near Burlington.
Some poor Indians laying here under their bark canoes, some going to and from the government house. And no we found many shore reduced to a very disturbed situation of mind, with with that destructive thing whiskey. So by their afflicting noise and appearance at the doors we decline going in, & upon inquiry found there was another stage 5 miles ahead. Here we left the green bank and rode on the sand, much like some of Jersey soil. We next & first come in sight of Captain Brout’s spacious house on a beautiful situation on the bank of the lake. We passed by it, a few rode to the Inn. Landlord’s name Bates. Civil people, but a very open house I think one foot open between some of the logs, where we could when in our bed look at the lake through these places, it being but a few roads from us, but took no cold. Here we first meet with Sammon. But to return early after we arrived here, we walked over to see the captain with a quiet mind as to myself. He received us kindly, his amiable looking wife also carried kind, but would not speak one word to us, which we understood was her usual practice courage towards white people. For my part my feelings became so disquieted while with them that I was glad to get away from them. I suppose that they have many Black houses, and I have since understood that he once put one
of his sons to death in his own defense. He was being a very vicious like child but I trust the quiet thereof is not entirely wiped away from his borders. Notwithstanding I understood he gave or offered himself up to authority. There is a considerable bank of stone washed out of the lake, some of them as large round as a small pewter plate, not far from what is called Burlington Island.

In morning Brant sent us over a basket of peaches previous to our starting setting out. Rode 22 miles through a wilderness belonging to Indians, up and down very steep hills and through swamps. Bated at or near a place called the credit, an outlet of the lake, so called where very fine salmon is caught. A large number of Indians inhabited round about of the Mississauga tribe, a very dirty uncivilized nation which occasioned it, disagreeable to see or meet with them but did not find that they behaved uncivil to any travelers. These people at the credit appear to be great enemies to the Indians. They buy their salmon by great quantities and other game, and pay them chiefly in whiskey, which is worse than nothing. The landlord acknowledged to us that the night preceding their lives was in danger by a large number being distracted with drink, and I marvel that some harm is not done by them in that way. We dined there upon salmon &
beef steaks, boiled eggs, etc. it was late in the afternoon before we left after dining, by reason of some of our horses not being so well able to travel as at some other times. Had 4 miles exercise, bad roads for mudholes. Then came to a nice building newly settled, owned by one Smith, here the Indian land ended and on to York. There was a two rod road laid out, and in riding 4 more came on night call at a small house. Man’s name Richard Wilson, had been a captain last war, where we had to beg for an entrance. Lodged on the floor on straw. The people did as well as they could for our horses and where disposed apparently so to be kind to us. Also, after we had an entrance granted us within the doors but they were poorly of for necessaries and convenience. Through favor we sleep pretty well.

In the morning started set out about sunrise, remain none in sight of the lake. Again rode up the shore over large squared stone, nice enough for a hearth. In 5 miles came to the umber ferry, not without some difficulty that the horses was got over. Mary & myself got over in a canoe, & 4 more miles ride got Yorktown. A very considerable collection of buildings, many of them handsome, generally framed of log, some brick. There is a garrison of soldiers kept here a goal
here is a ready market for all the provisions of the country as we understood hitherto that come to it or was in reach of it. We understood quite a few years since there was no house there, that there has been a rapid increase. After leaving it 11 miles, arrived at George’s Plato's to & breakfast. About 10 o’clock found them at home, treated us with much kindness. Dined about one, after having an opportunity in the family. Mounted our horses for Young Street. Soon fell into it and found a fine open road, with some good looking houses on each side. For some miles which road extends on beyond Friends settlement. And further in riding 15 miles arrived at one Richard Lippencott’s about sunset, whose wife thinks she is a member. They formerly moved from Shrewsbury in the wars to Nova Scotia, he having officiated as Captain. They were remarkably kind to us and horses, and furnished a table for us as well as we could for them and an excellent bed with curtains. She had the marks of a gentlewoman. One child, a daughter. He has the appearance of laborer. Talks of leaving them parts it not being agreeable to them. She showed us two certificates which she had procured in her travels from the people of the neighborhood where she had lived, setting forth her sober life and conduit as far as they knew of her to recommend her to her Friends again.
Notwithstanding she thought Friends had not testified against her.

In the morning rode 14 miles to meeting, it being on the street is called Young Street Meeting. Having an opportunity to forward word the preceding day, a very considerable number was collected. Dear Mary and James had a very full, open time I thought, & I felt quite quite easy to set under my own vine etc. The people seemed well satisfied at the conclusion. I trust there was some tendering impressions made on some minds, which with not be soon erased. Dined at Issac Phillips, Henry Widderfield and wife, several others came in afterwards. In the evening had an opportunity with Issac’s family, his aged mother living with him.

Issac in the morning with Irving Rogers piloted us to Joseph Randall’s, Henry Widderfields, dined. From there to Abraham Webster’s, Webstar’s lodged at William Londy’s after having an opportunity with their family and John Widderfield. In the whole 6 families. William’s wife lived in Father Thornton’s family some years, her name then Agnes Randall. They both appear to the growing in the best sense.

In the morning were at their father’s request, Samuel Londy’s—to Richard Londy’s—to (Phillip Phillip’s). Dined from there to William Howard & to David Wilson’s– to Issac Hitely, who had a short time before had his house burnt and all that was in it. a short time before we were there After those mentioned we got benighted in the
rain, extreme dark, but got through with difficulty to John Dunham’s, who’s wife appears to be under a tendering visitation. He also appears hopeful. They moved from Vermont county. Lodged under their roof comfortably 5 more families.

In the morning took an opportunity in J. Durham’s family with his brothers, who were invited to sit with us. Parted under a comfortable quiet—next to Joseph Pearson’s—to John Eves’s—requests 2 children–Henry Proctor has a Dutch wife, a tender woman. Dined with them, their (son in law Obediah Griffin requested) William Phillips, (Nathaniel Ganger requested) Aaron Tool, not members. Lodged at Wing Rogers.

Dear Mary poorly concluded to stay at our lodging and horse while we go to meeting, which was pretty full. At the close I felt as if I could leave them pretty quiet without such another opportunity, for which renewed favor. I trust I felt a degree of thankfulness. for and Returned to Mary, found her better but not able to go out much. James Wilson, Samuel, and myself rode several miles to visit the above mentioned Aaron Tool, whose house we had passed some days back. Returned in the evening.

Mary not able to ride, chooses to walk, as the family’s lays not far distant, it being desirous to be moving homeward as soon as we can. It is a trial to us all, however I thought I felt a degree of resignation to lay by freely for her relief, but she continuing to choose to walk we proceeded. Took Timothy Roger’s family, his two sons next not members nearby him.
(Issac Rogers not as yet members but under consideration) Wing Rogers, Henry Burnell, (Issac Hillingstowrth not yet in membership). Rufus Rogers and Asa Rogers where we lodged.

Here I may say that matter intrigued me with more reward than I looked for or thought deserved, which was humbling. May I praise his every worthy name, for his lengthened out mercy to one a poor unworthy creature in a distant land from many of my Friends & relatives. Dear Mary’s gathering more painful. She had a painful time last night with the addition of a pleurisy in her shoulder. Not able to set up out of bed. What a favor that I am strengthened to feel resigned to our allotment after rendering her all the kindness I have in my power in nursing etc. Upon a conference conclude to have some blood let, which accordingly was done, which gave some relief. I renewedly perceive that the everlasting shepherd of Israel can support the mind so as to alleviate close trials, which is one our companion being so much indisposed. Afternoon she appeared further relieved. James & myself rode in company with another friend to see Joseph Hill’s family, where I got necessaries for Mary. Samuel stayed with her in our absence. On our return found her no worse after having having such further attention
as appeared proper. She rested pretty well. In morning appeared much revived after taking some refreshment.

Sat meeting, which was held in same room she lay by reason of they’re being about to repaint the meeting house, which was thought to be a solid parting time, and and crowd as before perhaps more as the people appears to have open ears to hear and some of them tender desires to do right. Mary so recruited that she seems not to admit of a doubt of the propriety of riding 14 miles this afternoon home. Stayed with R. Lippencott’s wife, who came up to attend meeting together with Samuel to accompany her, was not given into without some considerable exercise of mind. But as she said and advanced as a reason thought she could be so much better done by there, I gave in to it and it proved her faith carried her through without receiving any inquiry. James & myself stayed behind to see some remaining families, which H. Widerfield & wife bore company in to Nathaniel Pearson’s. Robert Wood—Bejamin Pearson. Lodged at Henry’s.

Breakfasted. The morning proving very stormy, we did not leave until
after an early dinner, but to return to the morning felt comfortably housed. And a precious time we had with them and children, which I believe will not be soon forgotten by them nor us. Young Henry is a hopeful youth. The father and mother accompanied us about 2 miles to James Plato’s, not a member, whose wife is under tendering impressions. And also to see Jacob Hollenfield, just arrived in the parts, members. Here Henry’s wife & we parted, he accompanied on to Lippencott’s. An awful ride through the a wind of snow squalls. Here we overtook Mary and Samuel, found them brave. What a favor on both sides. Lodged.

Fine, cool morning, appear brave. Had a solid parting with Henry & the family under the canopy of quiet. We are in hope that Henry & wife may be of use there amongst the people, we put forward. In four miles ride came to Hollenfield’s, whose wife was a conrow. The desires to make satisfaction to her Friends for her outgoings, which we could not but encourage her in. Proceeded 6 miles further, called at one messer’s, not of our society but very friendly people. The wife met us first at the door with a bible in her hand, which at least wined her not to be a stranger to it. They some years past had lived near Jacob Londy’s. I felt very comfortable at leaving of them.
Farther on about 2 miles called at James Tuggles, a magistrate as we understood, four miles short of York. there there appeared great openness in him of towards friends. principles and greater kindness we could not desire to be manifested than that what was from him in particular.

After taking a nights lodging and having our horses well done by, we found a rainy morning. He appeared desirous it might continue, that we might be detained with them a few days, & said to our treasurer that when offering him pay that if he had not a mind to offend him to put up his money. But the rain had no discouraging effect with me, the mind being strengthened in a belief that that we should get through. it And after a few hours the clouds dispersed, & had a fine day bright day in a two fold sense. Dined sweetly on a log upon good roasted chicken and cake and other good things, while our horses eat their oats of the ground by us in the wilderness. Arrived in evening after riding about 44 miles at Bates’s on Brantsland, where we met with a kind invitation to breakfast with the great Indian. But as Mary was much fatigued we declined, or did not accept it. Pretty soon returned to our beds. In the night rained again, with an exceeding high wind, that I did not know but the roof would have gone. How good is our master to thus favor us, I thought in the proceeding morning as we started, was willing to ride in rain if we ought
be preserved from wind and as we was there, so now, far it fell before morning and clouds all dispersed Fine weather for traveling.

A calm inwardly and outward looks very pleasant every way to steer homeward, after riding up to Brants and acknowledging his kind invitation we put on & I got in to Samuel Beckett’s Short Hills, Pelham, about sunset. After riding upwards of 40 miles felt some fatigued in body but have got to good quarters to rest. All pretty brave here.

We met with James Thornton again again, who seems also brave. It is cause of humble thankfulness that we have been so preserved. Conclude to get our horses shoes repaired here, and feeling an aspiring for further labor here in this neighborhood propose tarrying over first day. Therefore Samuel Johnson & son James set out to ride to Newark and Queenstown, and interred meeting as again at meeting first day. Mary, James, and myself about same time after dining, set forward upon the above hinted service which we through favor poured successful in. viz.

In untangling the skein and winding it up followed the thread until it was wound up to our great comfort, and I believe to the relief of many minds, even the parties immediately concerned in so much that when we got to meeting first
so that when we meet at meeting on first day the gloom that had appeared on many countenance was removed and and cheerfulness instead. Therefore appeared I thought we had a seasonable parting under much sympathetic feeling, but previous thereto in the morning we paid a visit to one man who had lately been an active Methodist, and now had took a turn and attended Friends meetings, I thought to some satisfaction. We dined at John Taylor’s with several of the neighbors and set out with our faces homeward after taking leave of them with under a comfortable quiet, which I thought was a renewed favor to feel a portion of what I thought I felt at leaving my own habitation & from one move of to service to another. Jesse Wilson accompanied us to one William Londy’s near the falls & lodged, not Friends.

Fine morning, had a pleasant ride nine miles to Queenstown ferry. The water ran very rapid both ways, differently each side, and so deep that Benjamin Comly, the owner, informed me it could not be fathomed as yet. Its not half as wide as the ferry at Black Rock above the falls, crossed about eleven o’clock. Benjamin accompanied us 3 miles to the Tuskerook Village of Indians, where I felt my mind engaged. Previous to arriving there or knowing
that it would be in our road to have a religious opportunity with them, which upon consulting my companion, was agreed to, to make trial for to procure it which Benjamin assisted in. Their Chief being gone to Buffalo on business, & some others out hunting, was rather discouraging. But after about 2 hours about 40 men women and children met, and no stillness appeared. Even they lit their long pipe and smoked and talked, walked in and out until something was delivered by way of testimony, at testimony when they instantly gave great attention and appeared solid, even I thought it was fell over the meeting such a quiet that almost a pin might been heard to drop near one, and remained so until we broke it up. They do not appear to have any eyedia idea of worship in their meeting without minister. I supposed their minister instructs them so, and also endeavors as I have since understood to induce them against women speaking in their assemblies, and expect it was best that the Chief was not at home or we might have met with more difficulty. They have a very convenient house for the purpose of meeting. I left them composed in my mind with a belief that I had been endeavoring after faithfulness in the little and we on comparing notes thought that there was no harm done to Jew or Gentile. It affected my heart.
in taking leave with Indian Jacob, who had a few months before returned to them from serving an apprenticeship to Blacksmith within Chester County. He also appeared affected and said he many times felt very lonesome. Rode 6 miles to a very poor inn. Stayed overnight, several travelers being there, 12 in all. Very poor lodging. I set chief the night by the fire and repaired some of my things. & added a little to my journal, and scarce room to even set near the fire for mens feet.

Mounted our horses before sunrise. Rode 42 miles to Bestow. Lodged again at the Ellicott’s, kindly entertained. Set out again about nine o’clock. Rode about 25 miles to Genesee River to Widow Berry’s. Many not being well, we conclude to stop until morning. When she appeared some better, rode 22 miles to Jacob Smith’s, Mud Creek. Stopped all night.

In morning rode 7 miles to meetings, left our horses at Nathan Comstock’s, he with his wife elderly. As we thought favored with a pretty solid one the people appeared attentive generally. Lodged at Abraham Lap’s house where Elias Hicks, Daniel Titus, & Simeon Brown came in about twice, light on their return from a visit to their members in Canada, at the bay of County and country of Adulsets-town,
which was very cordial to our minds to meet with them in this distant land from our aquaintances, which appeared to be mutual. Some of their neighbors were invited in, and we had a comfortable time together, and favored to calmly retire to our beds. Rainy night.

Morning. Also towards noon, held up, we took leave of our said Friends and set homeward about 6 miles. Dear Mary feeling not able to proceed stopped at Benjamin Haines who has a precious daughter, himself on a committee to offer a meeting at six, is under their care in company with Caleb Macember & wife. The public well approved, they not being provided with conveyances to accommodate. We moved on 2 miles further to lodge to Nathan Harrington’s, he out a member among us two years since, wife a rigid Baptist. I took him to be pretty well grounded–and felt much sympathy for him. There appears to be a lively growing meeting here in this neighborhood.

In the morning, dear Mary some relieved from pain but not able to travel yet. The rest of us return 6 miles to meeting, and I believe had no cause to repent, so during dined with Mary at the above said place. The afternoon she was considerably revived. Several neighbors came in,
which season I hope may tend to profit my mind. Notwithstanding tried, yet I trust a little strength is vouchsafed to stand still. In the evening, William Shotwell with their family came in about dusk, on their way to Pelham in Canada to settle. All in pretty good health.

In the morning we took an affectionate leave of each other, and commanded another to that, that is able to build us up on the immovable rock Christ Jesus. After mounting our horses proceeded riding 4 miles. Came to Canadackwaytown. Many fine buildings, on an eminence in sight of the lake from which the town derives its name. 15 miles from further on arrived at Judge Potter’s, an elegant building, the country improving fast. He, not at home, his wife very kind used all the means she could for us to tarry with them all night after getting a good dinner. Notwithstanding we thought best to move on. I parted with her with reluctance. Met the Judge a few miles on, 2 1/2 miles got to where Morris Shepherd lives. Samuel Johnson & James Thornton stopped with them
overnight. We proceeded on 2 miles to W. Lee’s by Waggoners mill, were kindly received. Previous to getting here I had felt some moving respecting a meeting which increased on arriving at the place so as to believe it safest to upon consulting my companions to have notice given accordingly.

Next day about 1 o’clock the people met a pretty large company, diverse of Jemima Wilkenson adherents. Amongst them I found much relief to my mind after it & have cause to believe it was the like case without companions, the peoples parted with us very respectfully. Have renewed cause to say we serve a kind master who reds rewards amply for our labors. as Thomas Lee and wife could not freely give us up, we agree to tarry until morning. Which appeared right, as we left the place in as much sweetness as perhaps we had done elsewhere Boarded 12 miles on the way at a comfortable inn by name Teeple. Here Dear Mary outstripped us all in riding, the mind being relieved the body was assisted to persevere on in 14 more to Bartlet’s. Dined at a decent good table, kindly religious landlady. To Dobson’s 11 miles, lodged pretty good stage.

Partook of very good
venison steaks & in morning rode down Conhocton river 12 miles to painted post. Crossed the Conhocton and then rode down the Conisteer 4 miles. Fed & rode 18 miles through a rough looking loose people, horse racers, etc. Little sense of religion with some. I leaved to one Berry’s, some methodists had held some meetings with them at later time, and I am not able to say much against them going where there is no religion established as there away. Along the Connestere in crossing the river many times through the day. I was very much fatigued, but the mind through favor preserved in a calm that I have to believe that the wilderness may be to us a pleasant place. We did not leave them without making some remarks upon what we thought of the right way for Christians to walk, which they appeared to take kind.

In the morning left and ride 12 miles by ½ past nine to breakfast to Joseph Ross, his wife, Thomas Lee’s daughter, and rested a while here. Then rode 8 miles to better camp, by name Blaze. Lodged under considerable exercise.

In morning rose early and breakfasted. Mounted about six o’clock. After going a few roads found my previous exercise, and then led to some advice to the people left behind. I let my companions know and turned back and discharged delivered what I thought was given me, for which I found relief to my depressed mind, and with quietness pursued over the mountains Chestnut Ridge. Extreme rocky & muddy. Allegany 10 miles to Black house. Fed and proceeded 19 miles more, and over Trout Run 30 times in three miles. At the end, thereof turned off to Pine Grove. 6 miles to John Wilson’s. Chief of the way on the Allegheny, such a road I had not before rode for such a distance of continual assent. On the side thereof a cut road, so that we were quite in the clouds for a considerable time. We felt glad to get to a house.

Attended meeting next day. Very rainy but diverse attended of the members and some walked on foot. I was not sorry our lots were cast there. Dined at Moses Starn’s,
where we saw a young man who had been reduced very low with the bilious fever. The family had taken it in moving there from Maryland up the Susquehannah, waters being very low, and seven had died out of thirteen, his father and mother, Lancasters by name. The weather remaining unfit to travel for some of us, rode over to Israel Londy’s to lodge. His wife, Job Hugh’s daughter, a hopeful young couple. It is truly animating to meet with such, although they be by far too few, considering the number of our Israel that are called by the name.

Fine clear morning. Mounted our horses. Dear Mary seems pretty brave to what she sometimes has been called. At another.Londy’s on our way in riding 13 miles, arrived at William Ellis’s about one o’clock hoping we might be permitted to keep our faces homeward, but feeling my mind brought under a fresh exercice respecting going 30 miles over the Allegany to Ecroyd’s settlement.

I dwelt under it until next morning, when it was proposed for us to set forward homewards. I then spread my
exercise, first to Dear Mary. She with the others early after agreed to bear company, and set out immediately after breakfast. It was a dull looking time, the clouds being very thick, & the air cold, it soon began to snow. We rode all the way in & arrived a little after night at James Ecroyd’s.

Had a meeting appointed next day at 2 o’clock, about 30 members with others assembled at Jesse Haines’s, and I believe we, of the visitors, was thankful that we had been helped to give up to go there. Lodged after meeting with J. Haines & spent an agreeable evening there I hope there will be a regular meeting held there before they lose much more time.

Next morning, mounted and pressed through the snow. Quite a sharp morning, and may say I got along, considering the weather, much better than I expected. Landed again at William Ellis’s in evening of our Quarterly at Abington, which we repeatedly found to be as head quarters, and took another nights rest at this comfortable place.

Morning. Previous to our mounting our horses, feeling impressions to set down in solemn quiet, with the parents and children it was attended to, at which time some of the secrets of the Lord was revealed and given to unfold. Which afterward Mercy acknowledged to be the case. Left them under a degree of a fresh offense. What poor women we are, and a humble acknowledgement that he the father of Mercy is good to his depending ones. Rode 20 miles to Fishing Creek got in to Edith Eve’s before three. Has three single daughters, named Elizabeth, Pricilla, and Ann, eldest about to marry. Worthy young women.

Meeting being appointed next day, we attended where there seemed to appear pretty clear vision and was enabled to clear ourselves. I believe after dining, Elizabeth & Pricilla & one of their brothers accompanied in to Catawissa. Had an awful time crossing Lippenhause 15 miles. Lodged at Benjamin Fields, his wife a motherly friend.

In morning visited John Joy’s, who appeared to have symptoms of consumption on him. A humbling time, has wife and several children. I felt much sympathy for them and in the opportunity I had to recommend resignation to them both, let the event of his complaint center in life or death.
called at Elias Hugh’s, whose wife is Issac Bonsal’s sister. Attended their meeting which appears to be declining in Friends at Robert Fields’s. After, stepped in to see some Friends by name of Ellis, he lame. She much affected with rheumatism. A comfortable time, tender minded Friends. Rode same evening to Job Hugh’s under much depression of spirit respecting Berwick.

In morning, made my exercise known. Job Hughs & wife kindly offering to bear company with James Wilson. It opened the way for Dear Mary to continue forward gently, as she was not able to endure much hardship in riding at that time. Therefore I exercised her. James Thornton remained with Mary & Samuel, and we turn about, and in going over a very rough road, got there as near way in 16 miles, about two o’clock put up at Andrew Spinott’s, a Dutchman.

Had a meeting appointed next day at 10 o’clock. Had a very exercising time there. One of his daughters, it afterwards appeared, had concluded to marry the afternoon after we left here. I fully believed things were much
out of the right line. There was a considerable collection of people and considerably communicated by some of my friends, but I come away much depressed from the neighborhood. Returned to Job Hugh’s same evening.
Took leave of them and mounted about 6 o’clock, and rode about 27 miles over the mountains to Thomas Write’s same evening. Kind Friends, very very simple.
Had a meeting at Maiden Creek next day, 5 miles to it. Dined at Thomas Lightfoot’s. He kindly took me with some of his family to visit Uncle Stan, an elderly Friend. Returned with him to lodge.

In morning, 9 miles to Readen meeting, which appears very weak, but I was not without hope of a revival. Dined at William Spickmans, visited one William’s family. Has a hopeful daughter, not a member here. James Wilson left us and Penrose while William Lightfoot accompanied us into the neighborhood of Exetor. Lodged at Benjamin Write’s.

11 miles ride, worthy friends. 3 miles to meeting. Some lively, spirited Friends there. Dined at Mordecai Lee’s, whose wife has a few words by way of testimony. They both accompanied us to Pots Grove. Lodged at William Ive’s.

After riding 11 miles, in morning attended their meeting
which appears small, where-in inward silent worship was recommended. I hope it ended well. Dear Mary I thought was favored in it. Dined at Christopher Garrett’s, his wife’s sister not at home, by name of Mcclintock, who owned the house. Took leave of our Friend Mordecai Lee & wife & set forward, William Ives in company. 60 miles to Moses Hobson’s, where we was comfortably housed.

A meeting was appointed next afternoon at 2 o’clock accordingly. Friends meet generally with some others, which season tended to the relief of my own mind, and I hope not to the dishonor of the truth.
Spent a pleasant forenoon with the ancient Friend, Moses’s mother, aged near 78 years, not able to get to meetings. Has an excellent memory. A lively, spirited Friend. Lodged at Robert Harper’s.

Morning, moved forward to Plymouth. Visited several Friends in their families, and next day attended a large meeting. There collected an account of a funeral of a young married man, the evening of which day I reached home and found my family &
Friends in well health, for which favor I feel thankful.
